erode

/ih-ROHD/ — rhymes with road · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To erode is to gradually wear away, usually because of the steady action of water, wind, or another force over time.

Centuries of wind eroded the cliff into a graceful arch.

Example

Year after year, Atlantic waves hammered the shoreline, gradually eroding the sandy beach until only exposed rock remained.

The wearing away here is slow and relentless, driven by natural forces — that grinding action from water is exactly what erode names. Because the change happens gradually over time through the mechanical action of water, erode is more precise than simply saying the beach 'changed' or 'shrank.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

weather: To weather is to change slowly under sun, wind, and rain — wood grays, paint fades, stone roughens. The thing stays where it is, only its surface altered. To erode goes further: the material itself is carried away, grain by grain, until the shape changes.

corrode: To corrode is to eat something away through chemical action — rust chewing through iron, acid pitting a pipe. To erode is mechanical instead of chemical: water, wind, or footsteps grinding material away bit by bit. Chemistry corrodes; moving forces erode.

abrade: To abrade is to scrape or rub a surface away roughly, the way sandpaper bites into wood — quick, harsh, and close up. To erode is slower and larger: a force like water or wind wearing away soil or rock over years, not minutes.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

strengthen: to make something stronger and more solid

reinforce: to add support so something holds firm

Where it sits · how much material is lost — scuff → wear → disintegrate → erode

scuff vs. erode: Scuff is the mildest of these words — a light surface scrape on a shoe — nothing like erode, which keeps wearing material away year after year.

wear vs. erode: Wear is stronger than scuff but still weaker than erode: stone steps wear smooth from footsteps, but a coastline erodes, losing real ground to the relentless sea.

disintegrate vs. erode: Disintegrate is the extreme end of the scale; a cliff that erodes loses a little rock at a time, but one that disintegrates crumbles apart entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: away, out (form of ex-) (Latin)

Root — rod

Root — rod: to gnaw (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: E- (a form of ex-) means 'away' and the Latin root rod- means 'to gnaw' — so to erode is literally 'to gnaw away,' the perfect picture of wind, water, or doubt taking tiny bites out of something until it wears down.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / technical

Erode is the precise term when describing the wearing away of rock, soil, or landscape features by water, wind, or other geological forces. For everyday wear and tear on objects, simpler words like 'wear,' 'wear out,' or 'deteriorate' are clearer and more natural.
